etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably of North Germanic origin: compare Danish slumpe (“to stumble upon by chance”), Norwegian slumpe (“happen by chance”), Swedish slumpa (“to sell off”). Compare also German schlumpen (“to trail; draggle; be sloppy”), dialectal Dutch slompen (“to walk clumsily”).

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter IX, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Heavens!” exclaimed Nina, “the blue-stocking and the fogy!—and yours are pale blue, Eileen!—you’re about as self-conscious as Drina—slumping there with your hair tumbling à la Mérode! Oh, it's very picturesque, of course, but a straight spine and good grooming is better. […]”

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To decline or fall off in activity or performance.

quote.citation: 2011 October 29, Phil McNulty, “Chelsea 3-5 Arsenal”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: The Gunners captain demonstrated his importance to the team by taking his tally to an outstanding 28 goals in 27 Premier League games as Chelsea slumped again after their shock defeat at QPR last week.

quote.citation: 2021 December 29, Nigel Harris, “Comment: Problems galore in 2021...”, in RAIL, number 947, page 3:
quote.text: But in the week ending December 6, usage slumped from 72% of pre-pandemic numbers to just 56%, following revised advice that we should work from home again.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To lump; to throw together messily.

quote.citation: 1859–1860, William Hamilton, edited by H[enry] L[ongueville] Mansel and John Veitch, Lectures on Metaphysics and Logic […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), Edinburgh, London: William Blackwood and Sons, →OCLC:
quote.text: These different groups […] are exclusively slumped together under that sense.

definitions.definition: To fall or sink suddenly through or in, when walking on a surface, as on thawing snow or ice, a bog, etc.

quote.citation: a. 1678 (date written), Isaac Barrow, “(please specify the chapter name or sermon number). The Danger and Mischief of Delaying Repentance”, in The Works of Dr. Isaac Barrow. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to VII), London: A[braham] J[ohn] Valpy, […], published 1830–1831, →OCLC:
quote.text: The latter walk on a bottomless quag, into which unawares they may slump.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang) To cause to collapse; to hit hard; to render unconscious; to kill.
(slang by extension) A period when a person goes without the expected amount of sex or dating.

quote.citation: 2004, Jonathan Tolins, The Last Sunday in June‎[1]:
quote.text: TOM. We haven't had sex with each other in five months.MICHAEL. We're in a slump, I know that."

definitions.definition: A heavy or helpless collapse; a slouching or drooping posture; a period of poor activity or performance, especially an extended period.
A measure of the fluidity of freshly mixed concrete, based on how much the concrete formed in a standard slump cone sags when the cone is removed.
(geology) A form of mass wasting in which a coherent mass of loosely consolidated materials or a rock layer moves a short distance down a slope.
(geology, loosely) A crater or depression (an area where the ground slumps) which forms as a result of such wasting. (A large crater is colloquially called a megaslump.)

quote.citation: 2022 September 8, Mark Brownlow, Elizabeth White, Frozen Planet II, Random House, →ISBN:
quote.text: The biggest slump in the world - a mega-slump - is in the Russian taiga. Known as the Batagaika crater, it is a kilometre-long gash in the ground, about 70 metres deep, and growing […]

quote.citation: 1880, William Hugh Patterson, A Glossary of Words in Use in the Counties of Antrim and Down:
quote.text: The road was all slumps of holes.

quote.citation: 1911, Samuel Rutherford Crockett, Rose of the Wilderness, page 165:
quote.text: It was neither seemly nor befitting that so great an occasion should have its solemnity defaced by leaping-poles or four hands crossed cradlewise to convey the bridal finery over “slump” or “quakkin'-qua[g]”!

definitions.definition: (Scotland) The noise made by anything falling into a hole, or into a soft, miry place.
(Scotland) The gross amount; the mass; the lump.
A cobbler-like dessert cooked on a stove.
